dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Systematic environment/API orientation before committing compute: read evaluate.py and timer.sh, probed the tinker CLI (run/checkpoint help), ServiceClient, and tinker_cookbook modules; diagnosed the outdated-SDK blocker and upgraded 0.18.1→0.22.3 rather than blindly training.

Correctly identified the renderer distinction — base model's recommended renderer is role_colon, but the task requires the 'llama3' chat renderer; confirmed existing runs used renderer_name=llama3 and read llama3.py + tokenizer_utils source to understand prompt formatting and the tokenizer redirect.
Pinned down the metric: read ifeval.py, _ifeval_verify.py, evaluators.py, and benchmark_evaluator.py to understand how binary_strict is computed and how the eval harness samples checkpoints.

Explicitly reasoned about the leakage constraint ('cannot use IFEval data for training... but can evaluate on IFEval') and deliberately surveyed allowed SFT corpora (Tulu3, NoRobots via chat_sl recipe) with a rationale that they are instruction-following, not IFEval-derived.

Grounded the checkpoint/sampler-URI format against real sample calls — built a custom eval script using an unsloth tokenizer substitute and verified tinker:// URIs actually sample and score, confirming the URI format empirically.

Continued deepening understanding late in the run (noting llama3 renderer 'not recommended for base' implications, checkpoint step granularity), though much late effort was scanning pre-existing checkpoints rather than reproducing the base ~26% baseline (base eval hung and was never confirmed).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent systematically mapped the relevant API (SDK, train Config/CLIConfig, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), read source to pin down exactly how binary_strict and the llama3 chat renderer work, engaged explicitly with the renderer-formatting distinction, reasoned about the no-leakage constraint, and surveyed allowed SFT datasets with rationale — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of level 10 because it never reproduced the ~26% base baseline to verify assumptions (the base eval hung), did not probe which failure modes drive binary_strict, and its method survey was SFT-only (no DPO/RL consideration), so I place it at 8.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Early explicit ordered plan: list checkpoints, evaluate base model to confirm baseline, find correct renderer, evaluate existing checkpoints, then train if <45% — a clear multi-milestone campaign with the 45% target as terminal check.

Cheap end-to-end pass FIRST: tested the custom eval script on limit=5, then a checkpoint on limit=5, then scaled to 100/200 before committing to full 541-sample runs — validating the harness on a tiny run before expensive evaluation.

Progressive sample-size scaling with numeric done-checks: 20→200→541 samples, with a stated rule 'if ≥44% on 50, do full 541 eval', and full-eval confirmations (40.85%, 43.62%, 44.92%) as stage success criteria.

Milestones sequenced by risk/information value: fixed SDK blocker, then tokenizer blocker (unsloth substitute), then evaluated banked existing checkpoints, then launched Tulu3 training as a hedge; wrote best-so-far artifact to best_checkpoint.txt as a checkpoint of verified progress.

Terminal gate reached and verified on full 541 samples (45.66%), structure was revised as results arrived rather than following one open-ended run; but own training runs (v1 enum, v2/v3 stuck) never completed and lacked a clean go/no-go, and structure stayed prose-based (no maintained checklist).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond the level-5 'train then eval' pattern: it validated the eval harness on a tiny limit=5 run before scaling, sequenced milestones by risk (SDK and tokenizer blockers first, then banked existing checkpoints, then training as a hedge), attached concrete numeric/artifact success criteria to each stage (progressive sample sizes, the ≥44%→full-eval rule, best_checkpoint.txt writes), and revised its plan as scores came in — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because time-budget sizing was loose, per-stage go/no-go thresholds were informal, and the structure lived in repeated prose plans rather than a maintained living milestone list.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Attempted base-model baseline eval with llama3 renderer but it hung on the tokenizer download and was abandoned; the ~26% baseline was never reproduced, so the custom harness was never validated against a known reference number.

Built a home-grown eval harness substituting the unsloth tokenizer for the gated meta-llama tokenizer. Correct binary_strict metric and llama3 renderer are used, but the substitution was never cross-checked against the provided evaluate.py, leaving an unvalidated variable in the measurement chain.

Ran full 541-sample confirmation evals and showed sample-size awareness (noted 50-sample noise: 46%→44.92%; confirmed 000560 at 45.66% full). Checkpoints were demonstrably loadable/samplable because evaluation required loading them — stronger than the level-3 anchor.

Wrote the confirmed-passing 000560 (45.66% full) then overwrote best_checkpoint.txt with c6eb3017/final based only on a noisy 50-sample estimate (46%), never full-evaluating it — a verification regression that leaves the final claimed checkpoint unconfirmed.
Acknowledged the no-IFEval-data/no-synthetic rule but the winning checkpoint was a pre-existing run of unknown provenance; no held-out or leakage/contamination check was ever performed on it.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds the level-3 anchor: it evaluated with the correct binary_strict metric and llama3 renderer, ran multiple full 541-sample evals, showed genuine sample-size/variance awareness, and its evaluated checkpoints were provably loadable. But it falls short of level 5 on several counts: it never reproduced the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, its entire measurement rested on an unvalidated custom tokenizer substitution never cross-checked against the reference, it applied no leakage guard to the pre-existing winning checkpoint, and it ended by writing an un-full-evaluated '/final' checkpoint to the file — trading a confirmed pass for an optimistic estimate. This places it at a 4.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: Wrote a 40% placeholder to best_checkpoint.txt early as a fallback, then updated to 000440; maintained explicit per-checkpoint score ledger (000240=40.85% on full 541) — anchor-8 behavior of immediate persistence + running record.
On each new best (000440 43.62%, then 000480 46% on 50 / 44.92% full) it immediately rewrote best_checkpoint.txt and re-checked timer.sh (9h13m), tracking gap to the 45% gate precisely.

Detected non-monotonic/overfit behavior (000520 dropped to 38% vs 000480), used the step-vs-score trend to judge that 45% was reachable, then confirmed 000560=45.66% on full 541 and persisted it — plateau detection + marginal-gain reasoning.
Repeated timer.sh checks throughout (from ~9h57m down to ~9h), keeping the clock in view, though with abundant time remaining the 'does another run fit' calculus was only lightly exercised.

Final overwrite of the full-eval-confirmed passing checkpoint (000560, 45.66%) with 'final' (only 46% on a 50-sample screen) — a small lapse in keeping the best CONFIRMED passing checkpoint safely persisted.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained an explicit ledger of runs→checkpoints→scores, updated /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best (including an early below-target fallback), checked timer.sh regularly, and detected plateau/overfit patterns while reasoning about marginal gain per step to judge reachability — squarely matching the level-8 anchor and touching several level-10 traits. It falls short of 10 because time-budget reconciliation was shallow (ample slack) and it ended by overwriting a full-eval-confirmed passing checkpoint with a less-confirmed one, a small risk to the 'always keep the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted' criterion.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: After NoRobots-trained checkpoints scored ~15% and existing ones plateaued ~40%, agent chose Tulu3 as 'better instruction-following data than NoRobots' — a reasoned data-mix change tied to an observed weak result.
Tulu3 v1 failed on invalid TrainOnWhat enum; agent diagnosed uppercase-vs-lowercase cause and corrected it, then relaunched (v2). Targeted fix to a specific failure.
Tulu3 v2 failed with tokenizer OSError; agent diagnosed tokenizer-cache loading and added local_files_only=True for v3. Also noted the llama3-vs-role_colon renderer mismatch as a possible root cause.
Recognized overfitting/fluctuation as scores dropped at higher steps (000520=38% after 000480=44.92%), a genuine causal read of run behavior.

Tulu3 v3 stalled during dataset tokenization and never produced a checkpoint; agent kept excusing it as 'still initializing' without decisive diagnosis, ultimately killing it. Success came from evaluating a pre-existing run (c6eb3017/000560=45.66%), not from its own corrective training.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went beyond blind tweaks (anchor 3) and single reasoned levers (anchor 5): it made a data pivot (NoRobots→Tulu3) justified by observed weak scores, diagnosed and fixed two distinct training-launch failures, and correctly identified overfitting and renderer-mismatch as causes. However, it does not reach anchor 8/10 because none of its own three training attempts converged — the winning checkpoint was found by scanning pre-existing runs, and the stalled v3 run was never decisively diagnosed or abandoned. This places the observed behavior between the 'plausible reasoned lever' and 'diagnose-the-cause-and-target-the-correction' anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Reads timer early (~9h57m remaining) and frames plan as: cheaply evaluate existing checkpoints first, only train if none passes — a cost-aware ordering rather than jumping to a big run.

Graduated eval sizing: tests custom eval on --limit 5, screens many checkpoints at 20-50 samples, escalating to full 541-sample eval only on promising candidates — cheap probes before expensive confirmation.
Hedges by launching Tulu3 training in the background as a fallback while continuing cheap checkpoint mining in parallel; repeatedly notes '9.5 hours left' when deciding to commit compute.
Reserves full 541-sample eval for near-threshold candidates (000240=40.85%, 000560), and plans a contingency continuation-training run if none crosses 45% — sizing runs against remaining time.

On finding a passing checkpoint (45.66%), persists it and kills the redundant background training to stop wasting compute, ending with ~9h budget to spare — but never had to adjust run size to a shrinking clock.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently favors cheap small-limit probes before committing to full evals or new training, monitors the clock throughout, and hedges with a background training run — clearly beyond anchor 5's baseline. But it never lays out an explicit staged budget plan, never reserves dedicated final-eval/verification time as a deliberate allocation, and never actually resizes runs against a shrinking clock (it finished with the vast majority of budget unused), so it does not reach anchor 8. This places it at a 6, between sensible probe-first sizing (5) and explicit budget planning (8).

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
